headline_marked: [[OpenAI claims Navier-Stokes solution]] using AI, sparking data access controversy
headline: OpenAI claims Navier-Stokes solution using AI, sparking data access controversy
summary: OpenAI announced solving a 90-year-old Millennium Prize Problem, but a NYU professor claims OpenAI's AI model may have accessed his team's prior work.
details: OpenAI announced it found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a 90-year-old mathematical challenge related to fluid and gas flow. This problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million reward for its solution.

The company stated its internal AI model, more powerful than GPT-6 Astra and utilizing 10,000 concurrent agents, achieved this breakthrough. OpenAI began training this model on August 28th, noting its unprecedented performance in mathematical benchmarks.

The announcement sparked controversy as New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster had published findings on a related problem just one day prior. Buckmaster, working with Anthropic's Levent Alpöge, claims he contacted OpenAI after learning of their progress.

Buckmaster alleges that OpenAI's proof for the Navier-Stokes equation used a similar route to one he and Alpöge had been developing. He raised concerns about whether OpenAI's model had been trained on or accessed their drafts from Codex sessions.

OpenAI has attempted to address these suspicions, stating that "no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem." However, they added, "while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models."

Sebastien Bubeck from OpenAI reiterated that they did not see Buckmaster and Alpöge's work until its public release, emphasizing differences in their proofs and results. Buckmaster, however, countered on Mastodon, claiming OpenAI admitted to using training data from a period after his team found their result.

headline_marked: [[Meta launches Muse]], a personal AI agent for tasks and purchases, with privacy focus
headline: Meta launches Muse, a personal AI agent for tasks and purchases, with privacy focus
summary: Meta's new AI agent, Muse, automates tasks like emails and travel, and can even make purchases using Stripe's Link for secure transactions. It's rolling out today on iOS, Android, and WhatsApp, with a strong focus on user privacy and data isolation.
details: Meta has officially launched Muse, a personal AI agent designed to automate digital tasks. It's rolling out today for iOS and Android users via a dedicated Muse app and Muse.ai website, with WhatsApp integration also available. Users can try Muse for free, but extensive task automation requires one of Meta's AI subscription plans.

Muse is Meta's latest effort to compete in the personal AI agent space, challenging rivals like OpenClaw and Instinct. Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, the unit formed by Mark Zuckerberg, Muse aims to transform how users interact with the internet and Meta's product ecosystem.

The agent is designed for ease of use, allowing natural language prompts for tasks such as sending emails, booking travel, or selling a car. Muse can also make purchases on behalf of users, leveraging Stripe's Link payment infrastructure to issue single-use card numbers for enhanced security and guaranteed no-fee returns.

Meta emphasizes Muse's security and privacy features, debuting with a "Secure VM" architecture. This system isolates each user's activity in a virtual machine, separating untrusted web data from the agent's actions. A "Sentinel" system also prompts users for approval on sensitive actions, protecting against prompt injections.

Looking ahead, Meta plans to introduce "Confidential VM" for Muse, which will run in trusted execution environments. This advanced privacy feature will allow users to manage their own access keys locally, ensuring that no one, including Meta, can access their agent's virtual machine. This initiative is part of Meta's collaboration with Moxie Marlinspike.
